hooks.text: In 1799, a top scientist tried to cut this animal with scissors.
1799 was the year experts tried to cut this animal apart.
Scientists were so sure this animal was fake, they used scissors.

title: The 1799 platypus hoax that wasn't
description: The first scientists to see a platypus thought it was a hoax and tried to cut it with scissors to find the stitches.

beats.text: In 1799, a top scientist tried to cut this animal with scissors.
beats.visual: 1799 scientific illustration of the platypus from Naturalist's Miscellany

beats.text: British naturalist George Shaw suspected the first platypus pelt was a hoax.
beats.visual: Portrait of George Shaw, British Museum naturalist

beats.text: He thought Chinese sailors stitched a duck’s beak onto a beaver-like body.
beats.visual: Comparison image of a mallard duck bill next to a beaver tail

beats.text: Shaw actually cut the skin to find hidden threads, but found nothing.
beats.visual: Close-up of the duck-like bill of a platypus specimen

beats.text: The platypus defies logic as a monotreme, a mammal that lays leathery eggs.
beats.visual: Two small, leathery platypus eggs in a burrow

beats.text: Females lack nipples, so they secrete milk through pores directly onto skin.
beats.visual: Illustration of a platypus nursing young via skin pores

beats.text: It even hunts with eyes closed, sensing prey using electrical signals.
beats.visual: Illustration showing the electroreceptors in a platypus bill sensing a shrimp

beats.text: Males even pack venomous ankle spurs that cause humans excruciating pain.
beats.visual: Close-up of a male platypus venom spur on its hind foot

beats.text: No wonder the first experts tried to cut it apart with scissors.
beats.visual: A platypus swimming in an Australian freshwater creek
